name: Hemis Tsechu
when: June–July, 10th day of the 5th Tibetan month (lunar), two days
summary: Ladakh's best-known monastery festival: two days of masked cham dances in the courtyard of Hemis Monastery, honouring Padmasambhava, the teacher who brought Buddhism to Tibet. Villagers come in their best dress, and the courtyard galleries fill by mid-morning.
body: Hemis Tsechu falls on the 10th day of the fifth month of the Tibetan calendar, the day linked to the birth of Padmasambhava, known in Ladakh as Guru Rinpoche. For two days the stone courtyard of Hemis, the largest monastery of the Drukpa lineage in Ladakh, becomes a stage. Monks in silk robes and painted masks dance slowly to drums, cymbals and long horns, acting out the victory of the teaching over obstacles.

The dances follow a set order, with the masked figures of protectors, Padmasambhava's eight manifestations and comic characters who tease the crowd. Families from the Indus villages come in traditional dress, with women in perak headdresses studded with turquoise, and a small fair of stalls grows outside the gate. It is as much a community gathering as a show for visitors.

Every twelve years, in the Tibetan Monkey year, Hemis unrolls its great thangka of Padmasambhava, a huge embroidered hanging, on the courtyard wall at dawn. The festival is held at about 3,600 m, in full sun, so treat it as a day for patience, water, a hat and quiet respect.
tips: Arrive by 8–9 am to find a seat in the galleries; latecomers stand at the back.
Book Leh rooms and taxis early: Hemis festival week is one of the busiest of the year.
Do not step into the dance area, use flash or block the view of local families.

faqs.a: Hemis Tsechu falls on the 10th day of the fifth Tibetan lunar month, which usually lands in late June or early July. The exact dates are fixed by the monastery's calendar and announced in advance by Ladakh tourism. Check current status before you travel and book Leh rooms early for those dates.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Hemis festival?
faqs.a: Entry to the festival courtyard is usually free or covered by the regular monastery ticket, around ₹100 for Indians and more for foreign nationals, with the museum charged separately. Some years have reserved seating for a fee. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Hemis festival from Leh?
faqs.a: Hemis is about 45 km from Leh, roughly 1 h 15 min by road. Union taxis charge about ₹3,000–4,000 for the car on festival days, and extra buses run from Leh bus stand. Leave by 7 am, as traffic slows near the monastery.

faqs.q: Can I photograph the Hemis masked dances?
faqs.a: Yes, photography of the courtyard dances is generally allowed without flash. Do not enter the dance area, do not stand in front of seated families, and follow volunteers' instructions. Photography inside temples and the museum is restricted.

name: Dosmoche
when: February–March, 28th–29th day of the 12th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Ladakh's winter festival of the scapegoat, held at Leh Palace in the last days of the Tibetan year. Monks perform masked dances, and a tall thread-cross offering is carried out of town and burnt to drive away the misfortunes of the old year.
body: Dosmoche takes place over the last two days of the twelfth month of the Tibetan calendar, just before the Tibetan new year, usually in February or early March. In Leh, the dances are held in the courtyard below the old palace, and the town turns out in coats and fur hats to watch. Likir Monastery and Diskit in Nubra hold their own versions at the same time.

The centre of the festival is the dos, an offering made of wood, coloured thread and dough figures, built in the shape of a tall cross of threads. Monks dance around it with masks and drums, and on the final day it is carried in procession beyond the edge of town and burnt, taking with it the evil and bad luck of the year that is ending.

This is winter Ladakh: temperatures in Leh fall to −10 °C or lower at night, many guesthouses are closed, and flights are the only practical way in. It is also a chance to see a festival attended almost entirely by local families.
tips: Fly in and rest 48 hours before the festival; winter cold makes altitude symptoms feel worse.
Stay in a hotel with heating that is open in winter, and confirm it before booking.
Wear proper winter boots: you will stand on frozen ground for hours.

faqs.a: Dosmoche is held on the 28th and 29th days of the twelfth Tibetan lunar month, usually in February and sometimes early March. Exact dates move each year and are published in the Ladakh tourism festival calendar. Check current status before you travel.

The main celebration is at Leh, below Leh Palace, with masked dances and the procession to burn the thread-cross offering. Likir Monastery and Diskit Monastery in Nubra hold Dosmoche at the same time. Reaching Diskit in winter depends on Khardung La being open.

faqs.q: How cold is Leh during Dosmoche?
faqs.a: Very cold. Days in February are often around −2 to 5 °C and nights fall to −10 to −15 °C. Pack thermal layers, a down jacket, warm boots, gloves and a hat. Choose a hotel open in winter with reliable heating.

Yes. Dosmoche is a public religious festival and visitors are welcome to watch respectfully. Dress modestly and warmly, do not walk into the dance area, avoid flash photography and follow volunteers' directions. Most of the audience is local, so leave space for families.

name: Ladakhi Losar
when: December–January, 1st day of the 11th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Ladakh celebrates its new year, Losar, about two months earlier than Tibet, in the eleventh Tibetan month. Families clean and decorate homes, visit monasteries, light fires and lamps, and share food and chhang through days of winter festivity.
body: Losar is the Tibetan Buddhist new year, but Ladakh keeps its own date. The Ladakhi new year falls at the start of the eleventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in December, about two months before the Tibetan Losar. Local tradition links the early date to a 17th-century Ladakhi king who brought the celebration forward before a winter military campaign.

In the days around Losar, households clean and whitewash, make offerings at the family shrine and in local gompas, and prepare special foods. Relatives visit one another, and in many villages there are fire processions at night to drive out the old year. In Leh, the old town and monasteries are lit with butter lamps, and some villages stage masked dances.

For visitors, Losar is a quiet, cold time to see family-centred Ladakh. Leh is around −10 °C or colder at night, many hotels are closed, and you should fly in and rest. Be a respectful guest: it is a home festival, not a staged event.
tips: Fly in: road access from Manali and Srinagar is usually closed in winter.
Book a hotel open in winter with heating; many guesthouses close from November.
If invited into a home, accept butter tea or a small serving of food; refusing everything can seem rude.

faqs.q: Why is Ladakhi Losar earlier than Tibetan Losar?
faqs.a: Ladakhi Losar is celebrated in the eleventh Tibetan month, about two months before the Tibetan new year. Local tradition says a 17th-century Ladakhi king advanced the festival so his army could celebrate before a winter campaign, and the earlier date stuck.

It usually falls in December, on the first day of the eleventh Tibetan lunar month, with celebrations continuing for several days and sometimes into January. Exact dates change each year; check the Ladakh tourism calendar and current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens during Losar in Ladakh?
faqs.a: Families clean homes, make offerings at shrines and monasteries, cook festive food, visit relatives and light lamps. Some villages hold fire processions at night to drive out the old year. Monasteries perform prayers, and the atmosphere is family-centred rather than a public show.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting Ladakh for Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are comfortable with deep cold and limited services. You see Ladakh with few tourists, frozen streams and clear skies. Many guesthouses and restaurants close, so book a winter-ready hotel, plan rest days for altitude and keep your plans flexible.
